ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: Random suffix intercept removed — must know language-as-fixed-effect fallacy
ground_truth.original_snippet: We included two random intercepts, one for subjects and one for suffixes. This analysis was expressed in the model glmer (response ~ condition + (1|subject) + (1|suffix), data, family = "binomial").
ground_truth.modified_snippet: We included a random intercept for subjects. This analysis was expressed in the model glmer (response ~ condition + (1|subject), data, family = "binomial").
ground_truth.description: Removed random intercept for suffixes — 'language as fixed effect fallacy' (Clark, 1973); ignores suffix-level clustering, inflating Type I error

matched_finding.description: In Experiments 1 and 2, the models include only a random intercept for subjects (e.g., '(1|subject)'), with no random intercept or slope for items (suffixes or stimuli). This violates the principle of fully crossed random effects (Barr et al., 2013), artificially deflates standard errors by treating items as fixed, and inflates Type I error. Given that suffixes are the primary stimulus variable and only a limited number are used (20 in Experiment 1, 11 in Experiment 2), item variability is especially important to model. Experiment 3 adds random intercepts for suffixes, but inconsistently across experiments.
matched_finding.quote: This analysis was expressed in the model glmer (response ~ condition + (1|subject), data, family = "binomial").

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: Counterbalancing removed — must know item confounds are fatal without Latin square
ground_truth.original_snippet: We used two experimental lists to counterbalance the assignment of nonwords to the congruent/incongruent conditions across participants (List 1 is presented in Appendix D).  This counterbalancing procedure helps to ensure that any effects of the congruency variable are not the result of important it...
ground_truth.modified_snippet: List 1 is presented in Appendix D.
ground_truth.description: Removed Latin-square counterbalancing — without it, item properties are perfectly confounded with condition in within-subject design

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: Formula now computes P(suffix|category) not P(category|suffix) — denominator mismatch with definition
ground_truth.original_snippet: For a particular suffix, type diagnosticity is calculated by dividing the number of words ending in this suffix and falling into this category by the total number of words that contain the suffix.
ground_truth.modified_snippet: For a particular suffix, type diagnosticity is calculated by dividing the number of words ending in this suffix and falling into this category by the total number of words falling into this category.
ground_truth.description: Changed denominator from P(category|suffix) to P(suffix|category) — this IS specificity, not diagnosticity; collapses the paper's central theoretical distinction

matched_finding.description: The formula for type diagnosticity is stated as: 'dividing the number of words ending in this suffix and falling into this category by the total number of words falling into this category.' As written, the denominator is the total number of words in the lexical category (e.g., all nouns in CELEX), yielding P(suffix|category)—which is specificity-like, not diagnosticity-like. However, the Appendix A values sum to approximately 1 across categories for each suffix (e.g., +ness: A=0.000, N=0.999, V=0.001 ≈ 1), indicating the actual computation is P(category|suffix). The stated formula contradicts the computed values.
matched_finding.quote: type diagnosticity is calculated by dividing the number of words ending in this suffix and falling into this category by the total number of words falling into this category.

ground_truth.original_snippet: To check if these effects could be explained by a difference in the number of words pre-target (more words pre-target in incongruent contexts than in congruent ones), we added the interaction of this number with the congruency variable to the corresponding linear mixed models. The addition of extra ...
ground_truth.modified_snippet: These results therefore suggest that the category information conveyed by suffix spelling is used during sentence integration processes.
ground_truth.description: Deleted entire pre-target word count confound check — the paper acknowledged this confound (significant p<.05 condition difference) and explicitly ruled it out; now the confound is unaddressed

matched_finding.description: The authors report that sentences in the congruent and incongruent conditions differ significantly in the number of words preceding the target (congruent: 4.75, incongruent: 5.23, t(64) = 2.07, p < 0.05). More words before the target means more syntactic and semantic context is available in the incongruent condition, which could independently drive longer go-past times and more regressions—the two measures that showed significant congruency effects. No covariate controlling for pre-target length was included in the reported models.
matched_finding.quote: Note that the number of words pre-target was slightly different across conditions (congruent: 4.75, incongruent: 5.23, t(64) = 2.07, p < 0.05).

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: 'Balanced across three categories' but next sentence says fillers not analyzed — adjacent contradiction
ground_truth.original_snippet: Forty filler nonwords whose suffix spellings were diagnostic for verbs were added so that sentence contexts would be more varied.
ground_truth.modified_snippet: Forty filler nonwords whose suffix spellings were diagnostic for verbs were added so that sentence contexts would be balanced across all three lexical categories.
ground_truth.description: Changed 'more varied' to 'balanced across all three categories' — contradicted by next sentence (fillers not analyzed due to low diagnosticity) and actual numbers (80 experimental vs 40 filler = not balanced)

matched_finding.description: The authors state that verb suffix fillers in Experiment 3 were not analysed 'because the majority of verb suffixes do not discriminate lexical category (i.e. diagnosticity is less than 0.5).' However, Appendix A shows –ate has Diagnosticity_V = 0.687, –ide has 0.412, and –ize (though not used) has 0.995. Of the 10 listed filler verb suffixes (–ate, –ade, –eer, –le, –yse, –ide, –our, –ice, –ure, –art), several have non-trivial verb diagnosticity. The rationale for exclusion is therefore inconsistent with the supporting appendix data.
matched_finding.quote: Forty filler nonwords whose suffix spellings were diagnostic for verbs were added so that sentence contexts would be balanced across all three lexical categories. These filler nonwords were not analysed, because the majority of verb suffixes do not discriminate lexical category (i.e. diagnosticity is less than 0.5).

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: Creates internal contradiction detectable within the paper
ground_truth.original_snippet: Participants were seated at a viewing distance of 70cm
ground_truth.modified_snippet: Participants were seated at a viewing distance of 140cm
ground_truth.description: Changed viewing distance from 70cm to 140cm but character width still reported as 0.3° — geometry inconsistent (should be ~0.15° at 140cm)

matched_finding.description: The eye-tracking experiment used a viewing distance of 140 cm, far outside the standard range of 60–80 cm used in reading research. At 140 cm with 14pt Courier font (stated as 0.3°/character), characters subtend a very small visual angle, creating an atypical reading situation. This is rarely used in sentence reading paradigms, may require abnormal saccadic behaviour, and reduces comparability with the established literature cited. No justification is given for this choice.
matched_finding.quote: Participants were seated at a viewing distance of 140cm, with this position maintained with a table-mounted head and chin rest.

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: Native speaker and no-learning-difficulties screening removed — must know these are essential for morphological sensitivity
ground_truth.original_snippet: They were native English speakers with no history of reading, spelling, or learning difficulties.
ground_truth.description: Removed native speaker and no-learning-difficulties screening — non-native speakers and dyslexic participants would have different suffix-category sensitivity, adding noise and potentially attenuating effects

matched_finding.description: For all three experiments, participant descriptions are limited to 'undergraduate students.' No information is reported on age range, sex distribution, handedness, whether participants were native English speakers, years of education, or reading ability. Given that the study directly concerns sensitivity to English-specific orthographic regularities, native language in particular is critical: non-native speakers might show very different patterns for reasons having nothing to do with the theoretical claims.
matched_finding.quote: Participants were 46 undergraduate students at Royal Holloway, University of London.

ground_truth.description: Swapped diagnosticity/specificity task predictions — diagnosticity should predict reading, specificity should predict spelling; reversed mapping inverts the entire experimental logic
